Monday: Jeevan left the house at 8:30 with his laptop bag, as always, and told Amma he'd be late. He had been laid off on Friday. He spent the day in the public library in Jayanagar, staring at job sites, feeling like a fraud. Forty of them had gone. Somehow it still felt like it was about him.
Thursday: His cousin Shalini found him on a park bench at noon. He told her everything, voice cracking. "It was a budget cut, Jeevan," she said. "Your whole team. That's not a report card." She made him promise one thing: a timetable.
Two weeks later: Up at seven, applications from nine to one, a walk, calls to old seniors in the afternoon, a spreadsheet of every application. He still hadn't told his parents. But on Sunday, over dosa, he said, "Appa, Amma, I need to tell you something." His hands were steady.

qa.q: Where did Jeevan spend Monday?
qa.a: In the public library in Jayanagar, staring at job sites.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling on Monday, and why?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, like a fraud, because being laid off felt like a verdict on him even though forty people had gone.

qa.q: How did Jeevan start treating his job search like a job?
qa.a: He set a timetable: up at seven, applications from nine to one, a walk, calls to seniors, and a spreadsheet of applications.

qa.q: How might Shalini see Jeevan on the park bench?
qa.a: Shalini sees a cousin frightened and hiding, and wants him to understand it was a budget decision, not a judgement of his worth.

grounding: Being laid off feels like a verdict on worth and is hidden from parents; the protagonist tells one trusted person, sets a routine, and treats the search like a job.

passage: Asif, sit with me. You've been going out every morning in your office shirt, but I know you were let go. Your Ammi knows too. Let me tell you why I'm not angry. When I was twenty-four, I was laid off from a textile export firm in Surat, a woman of twenty-four in a job my whole family had boasted about. I felt like the company had held up a mirror and said, "Not good enough." For three weeks I pretended to go to work. I sat in a temple courtyard every day, pretending. Then my friend Kokila caught me there. She said, "The whole design unit closed, Urmila. Even the manager." I told her everything. She helped me make a timetable, and we went through the newspaper ads together every morning at ten, like it was an office. I found work in two months. So tell someone, Asif. That's what your Urmila-phuppo learned.

qa.q: Where did Urmila sit every day while pretending to go to work?
qa.a: In a temple courtyard.

qa.q: What did Urmila feel after being laid off?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and not good enough, as if the company had held up a mirror and judged her.

qa.q: What turning point in Urmila's story helped her move forward?

qa.q: How might Kokila have felt finding Urmila in the courtyard?
qa.a: Kokila was probably worried and sympathetic, and wanted Urmila to see that the whole unit had closed, not just her job.

grounding: An elder recalls hiding a layoff out of shame, then telling one trusted friend, setting a routine and treating the search like a job.

passage: "Damini, you asked how I told them. Badly, at first. Papa's pension doesn't cover their rent, so I send money every month. When I was let go, I didn't say anything for ten days. Then Maa rang and asked why my voice sounded strange, and I cried on the phone like a child. That night Papa called back and kept saying, 'What will we do? What will we do?' I felt accused. I snapped. Next morning I understood: that was fear. Love, just in an ugly shape. So I went home on Saturday, sat with them at the dining table, and put it all on paper: what I had saved, how long it would last, which firms I'd applied to. I asked Papa to help me call his old friend at the bank. He looked relieved to have a job to do. I'm Chetan, and I've learned they'd rather know than be protected."

passage: Vikas, you're angry about the cuts. Good. I was too. When I was twenty-five, I was a young woman in the accounts team of a shipping company in Kochi. In March they threw a huge party for our record year, with a band on the lawn. In May, they cut thirty jobs, mine included. I shook with rage. I went home and wrote a letter to the newspaper calling the directors thieves. My father read it and said, "Sleep first." Next morning I tore it up. Instead I wrote down three questions: how much notice would we get, what compensation was due, and whether the union could check it. I asked them in the meeting, slowly, one by one. The HR man had to answer in writing. My old boss later gave me a reference, because I'd stayed sharp but fair. Anger is fuel, Vikas. Your Shalini-ammachi burnt it for the right engine.

qa.q: When was the party for the record year?
qa.a: In March, with a band on the lawn.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel when the cuts came after the party?
qa.a: Shalini felt furious and betrayed, shaking with rage.

In the Leeds factory office, Kwame closed the door and lowered his voice. "Ada, the brake-pad test results from Tuesday. The third batch. Just log it next week, after the shipment goes."
Ada felt her stomach tighten. "The batch failed the heat test."
"Marginally. You're new, you've got the contract renewal coming up." He smiled. "I'm doing you a favour, keeping this simple."
She realised it wasn't a favour. It was pressure, with her job attached.
"I'm sorry, Kwame. I can't delay logging a failed safety test. I'll log it today."
Back at her desk, her hands were shaking. She typed him a short email: "Following our conversation at 3 p.m., confirming you asked me to delay logging the batch 3 failure. I've logged it today as required." Then she saved the number for the company's ethics line, printed on the poster by the canteen, into her phone. She had done nothing wrong.

qa.a: Log them next week, after the shipment goes.

qa.q: What was Ada feeling after the conversation, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt anxious and pressured, her stomach tight and her hands shaking, because her contract renewal was hinted at.

qa.q: Which steps protected Ada?

Three days before the district inspection, Principal Jyoti called Mohit, the attendance clerk at the municipal school in Nagpur, into her office.
"The grant needs eighty per cent attendance. Class 7 is at sixty-eight. Just mark the long absentees present for last month. Your contract comes up in April, na? I'd hate to lose you."
Mohit's mouth went dry. She said it kindly. That was what made it frightening.
"Madam, I can't change the register. If there's a reason the children are absent, maybe we can explain it in the report."
"Think about it."
That evening he wrote in a notebook: date, time, her exact words. He emailed a copy to himself. He looked up the education department's grievance email on the circular pinned in the staff room. And he told his wife, so he wasn't carrying it alone. It was not his fault that she had asked.

qa.a: Sixty-eight per cent, below the eighty per cent the grant needed.

Payal's articleship at the Mumbai audit firm had eight months left, and she needed the partner's reference. So when he told her to sign off the stock count for a client warehouse she had never visited, her first thought was: just do it.
She sat in the train home with the file on her lap, heart pounding. "Everyone does it" played in her head.
Her friend Ayesha, now working at a law firm, called. Payal told her everything. "Don't sign alone," Ayesha said. "Write down what he asked, and when. Your institute has an ethics helpline, call them tomorrow."
That night Payal wrote down the facts: date, client, the instruction, that she had not visited the warehouse. The next morning she called the helpline, then wrote to the partner: "I can't sign a count I haven't done. Can a senior who attended co-sign, or can I visit on Monday?"
Her hands were cold. But her name wasn't on a lie.

qa.q: What did the partner ask Payal to sign off?
qa.a: The stock count for a client warehouse she had never visited.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling on the train home, and why?
qa.a: She felt frightened and anxious, heart pounding, because refusing might cost her the partner's reference.

qa.q: What wise steps did Payal take instead of going along?

grounding: Fear of losing a reference makes compliance feel practical; the protagonist writes down the facts, consults an ethics line, and avoids being the only signature.

Week one: Zainab, a procurement analyst at the Hyderabad hospital group, noticed that the same supplier kept winning bids by a hair, and that Madhav, the purchase head, signed every one. Her stomach churned. Was she imagining it?

Week six: She submitted a report to the internal audit committee: twelve bids, the pattern, no accusations of motive. Then the waiting began. Colleagues seemed cold. She stopped sleeping well. She had expected stress, and she let herself feel it.
Week ten: The committee called her in. They had found more. "Thank you for doing this properly," the chair said.

passage:
Six weeks ago at the district hospital in Nashik, Rukmini, the ward in-charge, had initialled the hand-hygiene audit form that Mohit, the infection-control officer, filled in without watching a single round. "Ninety-five per cent, as usual," he'd said. She had signed.
Since then, every time a patient on the ward ran a fever, she felt a knot in her chest. She avoided Mohit in the corridor. She told herself it didn't matter.
It did. On Thursday she went to the medical superintendent's office. "I signed an audit form last month without the audit being done. I want to correct it, and I want a real audit on my ward." The superintendent listened carefully and arranged one for the next week.
When Mohit brought the next form, already filled, Rukmini handed it back. "Not this time. I'll walk the round with you tomorrow."

qa.q: What percentage did Mohit write on the audit form?
qa.a: Ninety-five per cent, as usual.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling after she signed the form?
qa.a: She felt guilty and anxious, with a knot in her chest whenever a patient on the ward ran a fever.

qa.q: How did Rukmini repair what she had done?
qa.a: She told the medical superintendent, asked to correct the record and have a real audit, and refused to sign the next pre-filled form.

qa.q: How might Mohit see Rukmini's refusal?
qa.a: Mohit may be surprised and uneasy, realising the shortcut is no longer accepted and he will have to do the real round.

grounding: The protagonist went along once with a falsified audit and feels sick; she comes clean, corrects the record and refuses a second time.
